chapters.title: The fruit lottery
chapters.hook: A random draw needs a complete guest list.
frames: List every possible outcome before calculating a chance.
Choose uniformly from apple, banana, orange, and pear.
Only one of the four outcomes is orange, so its chance is one quarter.
chapters.q: A uniform draw from four different fruits gives what chance of orange?
chapters.why: All four fruits are equally likely. Count one orange out of four.

chapters.title: The overlap trap
chapters.hook: Two invitations. One fruit. Don’t count it twice.
frames: An event is a collection of outcomes. Two events can overlap.
Suppose P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.5, and P(A and B)=0.2.
Add the first two probabilities, then subtract their overlap. The result is 0.9.
chapters.q: What is the probability of A or B in this example?
chapters.why: The overlap is included in both 0.6 and 0.5. Subtract 0.2 once.

chapters.title: Give randomness a number
chapters.hook: A random variable is a scoreboard for outcomes.
frames: Imagine tossing a fair coin twice.
Let X count the heads. Its possible values are zero, one, and two.
The four equally likely outcomes give probabilities one quarter, one half, and one quarter.
chapters.q: For two fair independent tosses, what is P(exactly one head)?
chapters.why: HT and TH both count. Two favorable outcomes among four.

chapters.title: New information. New odds.
chapters.hook: The yellow-fruit clue changes the game.
frames: A basket holds three red apples and two yellow bananas.
You learn the selected fruit is yellow. Only two outcomes remain.
Both are bananas. Given yellow, the chance of banana is one.
chapters.formula: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
chapters.q: Given yellow in this basket, what is the chance of banana?
chapters.why: Condition on the clue: ignore the red apples, then count within yellow.

chapters.title: At least one? Flip it.
chapters.hook: Sometimes the easiest route is the opposite event.
frames: Toss a fair coin independently three times.
The only way to get no heads is TTT, with chance one eighth.
At least one head has probability one minus one eighth, or seven eighths.
chapters.q: What is the chance of at least one head in three fair tosses?
chapters.why: Start with all tails: (1/2) cubed. Subtract that from one.

chapters.title: Count the wins
chapters.hook: A binomial counts successes under specific rules.
frames: Run ten independent trials, each with success chance 0.3.
The count of successes has a binomial distribution.
Its expected count is ten times 0.3, which equals three.
chapters.q: What is the expected number of successes?
chapters.why: The expected count is number of trials times chance per trial.

chapters.title: A random-sized crowd
chapters.hook: Poissonization makes some counts independent.
frames: Suppose the number of visitors is Poisson with mean eight.
Independently, each visitor chooses berries with probability one quarter.
The berry count is Poisson with mean two; the other count is independent of it.
chapters.q: What is the mean of the berry count?
chapters.why: Thin a Poisson count by multiplying its mean by the selection chance.

chapters.title: Average isn’t a promise
chapters.hook: Expectation is a weighted balance point.
frames: A game pays zero tokens with chance one half and six tokens otherwise.
Multiply each payout by its probability, then add.
The expected payout is three tokens, even though the game never pays three.
chapters.q: Must an expectation be a possible outcome?
chapters.why: An average can lie between the actual outcomes. This game pays only zero or six.

chapters.title: Split, then average
chapters.hook: Conditioning turns one big question into smaller ones.
frames: Half the days are busy with expected sales of ten baskets.
The other half are quiet with expected sales of four baskets.
Weight each conditional average by its probability: the overall expectation is seven.
chapters.q: What is the overall expected number of baskets sold?
chapters.why: Take the average of ten and four because the two day types are equally likely.

chapters.title: Only the present matters
chapters.hook: A Markov chain carries a very short memory.
frames: A fruit cart moves between a market and a park.
For a Markov chain, next-step probabilities depend on its current state.
Once you know where it is now, earlier locations add no information about the next step.
chapters.q: What determines the next-step distribution in a Markov chain?
chapters.why: The Markov assumption removes extra dependence on the past once the present is known.

chapters.title: Sample by wandering
chapters.hook: MCMC uses movement to explore a distribution.
frames: Build a Markov chain with the target distribution as stationary.
Detailed balance is a sufficient way to verify stationarity.
Convergence needs suitable conditions; successive samples are generally dependent.
chapters.q: Are successive MCMC samples generally independent?
chapters.why: A chain moves from its current state, so nearby samples are usually dependent.

chapters.title: How wobbly is it?
chapters.hook: Variance measures squared distance from the mean.
frames: A random payout is zero or four, each equally likely.
Its mean is two. Each payout lies two away from the mean.
The variance is four, and the standard deviation is its square root: two.
chapters.q: What is the standard deviation of this payout?
chapters.why: Square the deviations to get variance, then take the square root for SD.

chapters.title: Do they move together?
chapters.hook: Covariance reveals why variances don’t always just add.
frames: For any two variables with finite second moments, include covariance.
The variance of their sum is each variance plus twice their covariance.
Independent variables have zero covariance, but the reverse need not hold.
chapters.q: Does zero covariance always imply independence?
chapters.why: Zero covariance only rules out linear association in general.

chapters.title: The bell emerges
chapters.hook: Averages can look normal even when individual values don’t.
frames: Take a large independent, identically distributed sample.
If the population has finite, positive variance, the standardized sum approaches normal.
The standard deviation of the sample mean is population SD divided by square root of sample size.
chapters.q: If n quadruples, what happens to the SD of the mean?
chapters.why: The denominator is square root of n. Quadrupling n doubles that denominator.

chapters.title: Probability is area
chapters.hook: A density’s height isn’t a probability by itself.
frames: For a continuous variable with a density, find probability by area.
An interval probability is the integral of the density across it.
One exact point has probability zero, even if the density there is positive.
chapters.formula: P(a < X < b) = integral of f from a to b
chapters.q: Can a positive density at x still mean P(X=x)=0?
chapters.why: An individual point has zero width, hence zero area.

chapters.title: Stretch the scale
chapters.hook: Transform the axis; preserve the probability.
frames: Let X be uniform between zero and one, and set Y=2X.
The possible values stretch across zero to two.
To keep total area one, the density drops to one half on that interval.
chapters.q: What is the density of Y inside its interval?
chapters.why: The interval doubles in width, so the density halves to preserve total area.

chapters.title: Two dimensions, one chance
chapters.hook: A joint density spreads probability across a plane.
frames: For two continuous variables, integrate a joint density over a region.
Integrating out one coordinate gives the marginal density of the other.
For independent uniform variables on the unit square, a rectangle has probability equal to its area.
chapters.q: For independent uniform(0,1) X and Y, what is P(X<0.5,Y<0.5)?
chapters.why: The lower-left square has side one half and area one quarter.

chapters.title: Add the right family
chapters.hook: Some distribution families stay familiar under addition.
frames: Independent normal variables add to another normal variable.
Add their means and add their variances, not their standard deviations.
Independent gamma variables with a common rate also add, by adding their shape parameters.
chapters.q: Using mean-variance notation, what variance does the sum have?
chapters.why: Independence lets you add variances: four plus nine.

chapters.title: Package a distribution
chapters.hook: Moment generating functions turn sums into products.
frames: The MGF of X is the expectation of exp(tX).
When it exists near zero, its derivatives at zero give moments.
For independent X and Y, the MGF of their sum is the product of their MGFs.
chapters.q: For independent variables, MGFs of sums combine how?
chapters.why: The exponential of a sum factors; independence factors the expectation.

chapters.title: Which parameter fits?
chapters.hook: Likelihood asks which model best explains the observations.
frames: Observe seven heads in ten independent tosses with a common chance p.
The likelihood is proportional to p to the seventh times (1-p) cubed.
Its maximum occurs at p=0.7. An MLE is not a posterior probability.
chapters.q: What is the maximum likelihood estimate of p?
chapters.why: For independent Bernoulli trials with common p, the MLE is the observed success fraction.

chapters.title: Let evidence update belief
chapters.hook: Beta and binomial make an especially convenient pair.
frames: Start with a Beta(2,2) prior for a coin’s head probability.
Observe three heads and one tail in independent trials given p.
The posterior is Beta(5,3); its mean, and next-head probability, is five eighths.
chapters.q: What is the posterior predictive probability of the next head?
chapters.why: Add heads to the first shape and tails to the second, then use 5/(5+3).

chapters.title: The best squared-error guess
chapters.hook: Conditional expectation is a prediction rule.
frames: When X is observed, predict Y using its conditional mean.
Among predictors based on X, this minimizes expected squared error, assuming finite second moments.
Total variance splits into the variance of conditional means and the average conditional variance.
chapters.q: Which predictor minimizes expected squared error?
chapters.why: Use the average of Y among outcomes consistent with the observed X.

chapters.title: A cloud of variables
chapters.hook: Joint normality is stronger than normal marginals.
frames: A jointly normal vector has normally distributed linear combinations.
Its mean vector and covariance matrix describe its distribution.
For jointly normal components, zero covariance implies independence.
chapters.q: Does zero covariance imply independence for jointly normal components?
chapters.why: Joint normality is the extra condition that makes this implication valid.

chapters.title: The best straight-line guess
chapters.hook: Regression balances association and spread.
frames: The best linear predictor uses slope Cov(X,Y) divided by Var(X), if Var(X)>0.
Equivalently, slope is correlation times SD(Y) divided by SD(X).
This is a linear least-squares prediction, not automatically a causal effect.
chapters.q: If r=0.5, SD(Y)=4, SD(X)=2, what is the slope?
chapters.why: Multiply 0.5 by four divided by two.

chapters.title: More clues. One prediction.
chapters.hook: Multiple regression combines several predictors.
frames: Arrange predictors into a vector X with covariance matrix Σ.
When Σ is invertible, the best linear slope vector solves Σβ=Cov(X,Y).
Correlated predictors must be handled together; separate simple slopes usually won’t work.
chapters.q: Can correlated predictors generally be fitted by combining separate simple slopes?
chapters.why: Each multiple-regression coefficient accounts for the other predictors.
